passages.t: ‘The voice of the LORD’ in the storm
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm of David” (verse 1). The psalm opens by calling on heaven: “Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength” (verse 1).

Then a storm rolls in from the sea and across the land. Seven times we hear “the voice of the LORD”. “The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders” (verse 3). “The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars; the LORD shatters the cedars of Lebanon” (verse 5). Mountains seem to jump: “He makes Lebanon skip like a calf” (verse 6). Lightning strikes (verse 7). The storm reaches the southern desert: “the LORD shakes the Wilderness of Kadesh” (verse 8). And in the temple, “all cry, ‘Glory!’” (verse 9).

The psalm ends in calm. “The LORD sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD is enthroned as King forever” (verse 10). “The LORD gives His people strength; the LORD blesses His people with peace” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
This is a hymn. ‘Heavenly beings’ is in Hebrew ‘sons of God’ or ‘sons of gods’: the beings of God's heavenly court. Even they are told to bow. Then the storm moves from north to south: from the sea, over Lebanon and Mount Hermon (‘Sirion’ was another name for Hermon, Deuteronomy 3:9), down to Kadesh in the desert. The whole land hears it.

The cedars of Lebanon were the greatest trees anyone knew, used for temples and palaces. To see them snapped was to see a power no one could match.

Many scholars have noticed how close this psalm's language is to old Canaanite poems about the storm god Baal, found at Ugarit on the coast of Syria. There Baal's voice is the thunder, and he rules over the sea. Some think Psalm 29 takes words the neighbours used for Baal and gives them to the LORD. That is a comparison scholars make, not something the psalm says. Either way, its message to Israel was sharp. For people tempted to pray to Baal for rain (1 Kings 18), the psalm says: the thunder belongs to the LORD.

‘The flood’ in verse 10 is a rare Hebrew word, mabbul. Everywhere else in the Old Testament it names Noah's flood (Genesis 6:17). The LORD sat as King even over that.
passages.later:
When Jesus prayed, “Father, glorify Your name!” a voice answered from heaven, and “The crowd standing there heard it and said that it had thundered” (John 12:28-29).

On the lake, Jesus stood up in a storm and “rebuked the winds and the sea, and it was perfectly calm”. The disciples asked, “What kind of man is this? Even the winds and the sea obey Him!” (Matthew 8:26-27).

The psalm begins with ‘glory’ in heaven and ends with ‘peace’ for God's people. Some readers hear it in the angels' song at Jesus' birth: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace” (Luke 2:14).
passages.asks:
Psalm 29 asks you to let creation make you small in a good way. Next time a storm shakes the windows, try praying verse 3.

And notice the ending. The God of the thunder uses his strength to give strength, and his power to give peace (verse 11). You do not need to fear the storm when you know who sits above it.
